[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [542 U.S. 507](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-542/pdf/USREPORTS-542-507.pdf){.cite} [Decided June 28, 2004]{.cite} [Plurality opinion; judgment 6 to 3]{.cite}

**Holding.** The 2001 AUMF authorizes detaining individuals who fought against the United States in Afghanistan as part of or supporting Taliban forces, including citizens, for the duration of the relevant hostilities. A citizen detainee must nonetheless receive notice of the factual basis for his classification and a fair opportunity to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker.

**Question.** Whether the government could hold a U.S. citizen captured in Afghanistan as an enemy combatant, and what process he was due to contest that designation.

## Why it matters

The plurality read the [2001 AUMF](../statutes/aumf-2001.qmd)'s "necessary and appropriate force" to include detention as a fundamental incident of war, a reading later codified in the FY2012 NDAA. Its statement that "a state of war is not a blank check for the President" is a standard reference in debates over wartime authority.

## Status

Good law.

## Statutes at issue

- [2001 AUMF](../statutes/aumf-2001.qmd){.subj}. Held that the AUMF's authorization of necessary and appropriate force includes detention of enemy combatants captured in Afghanistan for the duration of hostilities.

Studied in [Unit 3: Deciding to use force](../study/units/war-powers.qmd).
